A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AFedPG, with matching algorithms and the same core global-convergence analysis. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original MuJoCo reward and timing experiments on Swimmer, Hopper, and Humanoid, including comparisons across agent counts and computing heterogeneity.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix A report original experiments on four MuJoCo tasks, including additional baseline comparisons, a lookahead ablation, and expanded computing-heterogeneity results.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same normalized server update, delay-dependent lookahead, trajectory sampling, and update-direction averaging. Expanded explanations and additional theoretical guarantees do not introduce a new AFedPG component.

E1.justification: v3 adds reported Walker2D-v4 evaluation to the three existing MuJoCo tasks; v1 only listed Walker2D hyperparameters. Appendix A.3 also covers both one-fast-agent and one-slow-agent timing scenarios, whereas v1 covered only the latter. The scenario names in v3 are inconsistently assigned.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds A3C and Vanilla, defined as AFedPG without delay-adaptive lookahead, at N=4 and N=8. The corresponding v1 Figure 5 compared only AFedPG and synchronous FedPG. These additions substantially broaden the empirical comparison methods.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes the listed Walker2D network from 256×256×256 to 512×512, timesteps from 512 to 1024, and iterations from 3000 to 5000. The reported Humanoid timing budget at N=8 changes from 80,000 to 120,000 trajectories, and heterogeneity sweeps add N=16. These reported setting changes do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 introduces a direct ablation of the central delay-adaptive lookahead component in Figure 4. Appendix A.3 also expands the existing heterogeneity analysis to two contrasting timing scenarios and additional agent counts, substantially extending the questions tested.

E5.justification: Both versions report convergence experiments over 10 runs using seeds 0–9, smoothed mean curves, and 95% confidence intervals. Repeating these details in v3 captions and extending the same reporting practice to additional curves does not change the statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds Walker2D outcomes and A3C/Vanilla comparison curves, and substantially revises the heterogeneity results. At heterogeneity ratio 9, v1 Figure 6 shows speedups of 5–8, while v3 Figure 6 reports values in the hundreds. The three original reward-versus-sample plots are unchanged. Changed budgets and inconsistent scenario descriptions prevent interpreting all differences as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v3 adds the FOSP criterion, Theorem 5.1 claiming O(epsilon^-3.5) sample complexity, and an Appendix B.5 derivation with different step-size schedules. The original global theorem and supporting assumptions and lemmas are largely retained and relocated. The new theorem states a final-iterate guarantee, while its proof bounds a weighted average of gradient norms.

C1.justification: v1 claims the first global-convergence guarantees for federated policy-based RL. v3 narrows that novelty claim to asynchronous federated policy-based RL and adds first-order stationary convergence as an explicit contribution in the introduction and conclusion. The main sample-speedup and asynchronous timing claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning malicious agents, compatibility with communication-saving techniques, second-order optimization, and experimental scale. It also discusses opposite agent-count effects in its two timing scenarios and explicitly explains policy-induced data heterogeneity even with identical environments in Appendix C.

D1.justification: v3 documents Walker2D's action/state dimensions and revises its network and training hyperparameters in Tables 2–3. The new reproducibility statement mainly points to existing pseudocode and experimental documentation; it adds no code-access resource. Software, GAE, and GPU specifications remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The FedRL discussion substantially expands its treatment of closely related work, including Chen et al. on federated PG, Ganesh et al. on global convergence with adversaries, and additional heterogeneous, multi-task, and communication-complexity research. This supports the narrower asynchronous novelty positioning. Table 1 also distinguishes vanilla from normalized PG.

P1.justification: v3 makes Related Work a standalone section, moves assumptions and key lemmas into Appendix B, and reorganizes experimental supplements into Appendix A. It replaces the standalone conclusion with Discussions, adds limitations and a reproducibility statement, and expands explanations of the asynchronous challenges and lookahead mechanism.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column ACM layout to a single-column format. Table 1 is restructured around FOSP and global complexity, task figures expand from three to four panels, timing plots gain additional comparator curves, and Figure 6 becomes two panels. Settings tables and the timing schematic move to the appendix.

improvement.justification: The added A3C comparisons, lookahead ablation, and explicit limitations strengthen empirical assessment and scope disclosure. However, the new FOSP theorem and appendix proof concern different convergence outputs, while the revised heterogeneity results introduce unexplained speedups in the hundreds and conflicting scenario descriptions. These unresolved issues affect important additions to the theory and scaling evidence, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
